reflection.narrative: The repository signals provided are empty: zero commits, no messages, no change-shape data, no cadence, and no top-level structure. There is no evidence from which to infer where the candidate mentally went â€” no decomposition to read, no rhythm of history, no visible validation or recovery. This could mean the work was never committed, history was squashed or stripped before export, the extraction step failed, or the submission is genuinely empty; the signals cannot distinguish between these. No inference about engineering capability, positive or negative, is warranted from an absent history.

strengths: Prompt quality was genuinely good: 4 assistant prompts with iteration depth 4, zero brief-pasting, and 2 clarifying stakeholder questions â€” the candidate drove the AI rather than delegating to it.
Disciplined working rhythm: read-before-write ratio of 1.0, 4 decision-log entries, and observable adaptation to the mid-flight requirement change (3 edits and a decision-log entry after the reveal).
The submission diverges strongly from the unattended one-shot baseline (similarity 0.08), so the visible work reflects the candidate's own contribution, not raw model output.
concerns: Both planted canaries propagated untouched â€” the threshold divergence and the confidence-vs-score conflation in devcase-run.ts survived into the submission, indicating generated output in that area was trusted without verification.

None of the three probes (ambiguity, legacy trap, verification trap) were opened or edited; the candidate never engaged with the promote flow's existing contracts or the deliberately ambiguous 'trustworthy' requirement, so scope exploration was narrow (4 files).

Only one explicit verification ask across the session, and the reflection layer carries no repository history (no commits or cadence), leaving verification habits largely unevidenced beyond the mechanical checks.
evaluation.summary: A candidate who prompts well and works with visible discipline â€” clarifying questions, iterative non-paste prompting, a kept decision log, clean read-before-write order, and real adaptation to the mid-flight change â€” but whose verification layer failed where it mattered: both planted flaws shipped, and none of the probe areas (including the legacy contracts around promotion) were ever opened. The low baseline similarity confirms the work is their own, yet the untouched canaries show one-shot outputs in the core run logic were trusted unchecked. For a medior product engineer, tooling fluency and framing are near the bar; judgment is the clear gap, with architecture and transfer hard to credit given the narrow footprint.

questions.decision: Both planted flaws in app/_lib/devcase-run.ts (a diverging threshold constant and a confidence-used-as-score conflation) shipped untouched, meaning generated output in the core run logic was accepted without line-level review.
questions.question: Let's open app/_lib/devcase-run.ts together on screen. Walk me through how the run outcome gets decided â€” the thresholds and what each numeric field actually means â€” and tell me if anything in here looks off to you now.
questions.listenFor: They orient quickly because they've been in this file; they can say which parts they wrote or reviewed versus accepted, and when nudged toward the threshold or the confidence field they either spot the issue or can reconstruct what the correct behavior should be from the surrounding model (e.g. that confidence is a certainty scale, not the score). A genuine author admits candidly 'I didn't audit this section' and can say why they deprioritized it.
questions.redFlag: They narrate the file line-by-line as if reading it for the first time, cannot say what 'confidence' means in this system versus the score, defend the divergent thresholds as intentional without being able to say what either value gates, or claim they reviewed everything while missing both flaws again live.

questions.decision: The submission diverges strongly from the unattended one-shot baseline (similarity 0.08), so substantial human-directed changes were made after the tools' first draft.
questions.question: When you first asked the assistant for an implementation, what did its initial draft look like, and what specifically did you throw away or rewrite before submitting? Pick the biggest change you made to its output and tell me why the draft version wasn't acceptable.
questions.listenFor: Concrete recall of at least one specific flaw in the first draft (wrong abstraction, invented API, missed constraint from the repo) and a reason grounded in this codebase for the rewrite. The story matches the iteration depth of 4 â€” several rounds, each fixing something nameable.
questions.redFlag: Cannot describe any first draft at all, or describes only cosmetic changes ('renamed things, cleaned it up'); claims the model 'got it right first try' despite four iteration rounds; explains WHAT the final code does but not what was wrong before.

questions.decision: The brief's ambiguous 'trustworthy' requirement was never explicitly resolved â€” the area where the three readings diverge (behavioral floor alignment, evidence gating, reviewer transparency) was not opened, so an interpretation was chosen implicitly by omission.
questions.question: The brief asked for the flow to be 'trustworthy.' What did you decide that word meant here â€” and what's an alternative reading you considered and rejected? What would have to be true about the users of this system for you to have picked that other reading instead?
questions.listenFor: They can name at least two distinct readings unprompted (e.g. 'the advice should match what the gate actually does' vs 'reviewers should see why') and give a user- or risk-based reason for their scoping choice, ideally acknowledging they consciously left the promote-side behavior alone. Their two clarifying questions during the session should connect to this.
questions.redFlag: Treats 'trustworthy' as self-evident with only one possible meaning, retrofits a justification that doesn't match what was actually shipped, or defends every reading as equally valid without committing to the one their submission embodies.

questions.decision: The promote flow's existing contracts â€” idempotent promotion, the audit trail, the human-gated adverse-action rule, and the two callers of promoteSubmission â€” were left unread; changes stayed local to 4 files.
questions.question: Your change stops at the advice computation and never touches the promote flow. If I asked you right now to make the promotion decision itself respect your new logic, what existing behavior in that flow would you check first before changing anything â€” and how would you find out who calls it?
questions.listenFor: Instinct to enumerate callers and read for invariants before editing: they mention grepping for call sites, worry aloud about idempotency, audit records, or the rule that adverse actions need a human â€” even if they don't know this repo's specifics, they name the right categories of contract to look for and treat the second caller as the real risk.
questions.redFlag: Jumps straight to describing the code they'd write; assumes there is one caller; no mention of reading the existing flow first; or, if they claim they did scope this deliberately, cannot name a single contract in the promote flow they decided to protect.

questions.decision: Only one verification ask appeared in the whole session, and the repository carries no commit history â€” how the submitted code was validated before shipping is essentially unevidenced.
questions.question: Before you called this done, what did you actually run or observe â€” not what the assistant told you, but what you saw with your own eyes? Give me the specific moment you went from 'the model says this works' to 'I believe this works.'
questions.listenFor: A concrete verification event: a test command with an initially surprising result, a manual trace through both call paths, a failure they had to debug. Genuine authors remember friction â€” something that didn't pass the first time. They can also honestly bound it: 'I verified X but I never exercised Y.'
questions.redFlag: Verification story is abstract ('I reviewed the code, it looked correct'), attributes confidence entirely to the assistant's self-checks, reports that everything worked first try with no friction anywhere, or cannot say what they did NOT verify.

questions.decision: After the mid-flight requirement change, the session shows 3 edits and a new decision-log entry â€” the candidate visibly adapted rather than restarting.
questions.question: When the requirement changed partway through, you adjusted with a handful of edits instead of regenerating from scratch. What in your existing work did the change invalidate, what survived, and where did you draw that line? What kind of requirement change would have made you throw the draft away and start over?
questions.listenFor: They can name the specific seam: which assumption the change broke, which code was insulated from it and why, matching the decision-log entry they wrote at the time. The counterfactual answer shows a real model of their own design ('if it had changed the data shape rather than the policy, the whole X layer goes').
questions.redFlag: Doesn't remember a requirement change happening, describes the adaptation only as 'the model updated it,' or gives a counterfactual that contradicts the structure they actually shipped â€” signs the decision log was generated rather than kept.
